nameStory: This tiny algae earned its "pin-cushion" name from its distinctive growth pattern — it forms dense, round, cushion-like clumps that bristle with short, branching filaments like pins sticking out of a sewing cushion. The bright green color gives it the first part of its common name, making it easy to spot against darker rocks and surfaces.
description: Green pin-cushion algae is a freshwater algae that forms small, dense, cushion-shaped colonies in clean streams and lakes. Each colony is made up of many branching green filaments that create a fuzzy, almost velvety appearance. The cushions are typically only 1-2 inches across but can be quite thick and puffy. Unlike the stringy, hair-like algae you might see floating freely, this species stays firmly attached to rocks and other hard surfaces underwater.

idTips.label: Cushion growth form
idTips.description: Forms distinctive round, puffy cushions that feel firm and springy to the touch, like a miniature green pillow attached to rocks

idTips.label: Branching filaments
idTips.description: Close inspection reveals many short, repeatedly branching green threads that give the cushion a dense, fuzzy texture

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Maintains a vibrant emerald green color that doesn't fade to yellow or brown like some other freshwater algae

idTips.label: Rock attachment
idTips.description: Always found firmly stuck to hard surfaces like rocks, logs, or concrete - never free-floating like hair-like algae

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Individual cushions rarely exceed 2 inches across and feel surprisingly solid when gently pressed underwater

habitat: Look for green pin-cushion algae in clean, flowing freshwater streams, rivers, and the rocky shores of clear lakes throughout New England. It prefers areas with good water movement and attaches to submerged rocks, logs, and sometimes concrete structures like dam spillways. This species indicates good water quality and is most common in cooler, well-oxygenated waters.

seasonality.spring: Growth begins as water temperatures rise, forming small bright green patches on submerged rocks. This is often the best time to spot new colonies as they contrast sharply with bare rock surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Reaches peak growth and size during warm months, with cushions becoming thick and lush. Look for the most vibrant green coloration during this season.
seasonality.fall: Colonies may begin to slow growth but remain visible and identifiable. Some cushions may start to look less dense as water temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Many colonies die back or become dormant under ice, though some may persist in areas with flowing water that doesn't freeze completely.

funFact: Despite being a simple algae, green pin-cushion algae can live for several years in the same spot, slowly building up its cushiony mass layer by layer — some large cushions may be decades old, making them among the longest-lived algae in New England waters!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with moss growing on submerged rocks, but algae feels slippery and smooth when touched underwater, while moss feels rougher and more textured. Remember: "Algae is slick, moss has grip."
contextualKnowledge: Note that this species has only been recorded once in New England, making it quite rare in our region. What you're more likely to encounter are its relatives or other cushion-forming algae that may look similar but aren't the same species.
compareHints: Green pin-cushion algae forms much more compact, defined cushions compared to its cousin graceful green hair algae, which grows in loose, flowing strands. While Cladophora albida also forms attachments to rocks, it tends to create more sprawling, less organized colonies rather than the neat, rounded cushions of the pin-cushion species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Graceful green hair differs from its Cladophora relatives by its exceptionally fine, silky texture and preference for the cleanest water conditions.
Compared to green pin-cushion alga, this species tends to be less densely branched and shows the characteristic whitish coloration that its relatives typically don't develop.
